A Russian amendment seeking to restore stronger language failed after a U.S. veto.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the way Israel was conducting its offensive was creating massive obstacles to aid distribution inside Gaza. Humanitarian agencies have warned that shortages of food, clean water and medical supplies are endangering civilians displaced by the fighting.

The war began after Hamas-led attackers entered southern Israel on Oct. 7, killing about 1,200 people and taking hostages, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent assault has devastated much of Gaza. The council's resolution also demanded the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages.

output.message:
Timor-Leste joins WTO as bloc expands to 166 members

GENEVA, Aug. 30, 2024 — Timor-Leste became the World Trade Organization's 166th member on Friday, completing an accession process that began in 2016 and bringing the small Southeast Asian economy into the global body governing trade rules.

The entry followed approval of its membership package at the WTO's ministerial conference in Abu Dhabi in February and subsequent domestic ratification. Comoros joined on Aug. 21, becoming the organization's 165th member.

For East Timor, well over two decades after independence, accession marks another step toward integration into the international economy. The country regained independence in 2002 after a U.N.-administered transition following Indonesia's occupation.

Membership binds the country to negotiated commitments on tariffs, services and trade legislation while giving its exporters access to the protections of the WTO system. The accession package includes transition periods for implementing some rules and provision for technical assistance.

The government faces the broader challenge of diversifying an economy heavily dependent on petroleum revenues. Coffee is a major non-oil export, but limited infrastructure and a small domestic market constrain business development.

WTO membership is separate from Timor-Leste's bid to join the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. ASEAN agreed in principle in 2022 to admit the country and granted it observer status, with full membership subject to a roadmap.

output.message:
CANBERRA, March 14, 2023 — Australia plans to buy U.S. nuclear-powered submarines and develop a new class with Britain under a defence partnership aimed at strengthening the allies’ presence in the Indo-Pacific as China expands its military.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, U.S. President Joe Biden and British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak unveiled the AUKUS roadmap in San Diego on March 13. Australia estimated the programme would cost A$268 billion to A$368 billion through the mid-2050s.

Under the plan, Australia would purchase three U.S. Virginia-class submarines beginning in the early 2030s, subject to congressional approval, with an option to buy two more. Britain and Australia would also build a new submarine, known as SSN-AUKUS, incorporating U.S. technology. The first Australian-built vessel is expected to enter service in the early 2040s.

The United States and Britain plan to rotate nuclear-powered submarines through a base near Perth from 2027, helping Australia develop the workforce and expertise to operate its own fleet.

The vessels will carry conventional weapons, not nuclear arms. Nuclear propulsion allows submarines to remain submerged much longer than Australia’s existing diesel-electric Collins-class boats.

China has opposed AUKUS, arguing that it fuels an arms race and poses nuclear-proliferation risks. The three partners say the programme will comply with their non-proliferation obligations, with Australia working with the International Atomic Energy Agency on safeguards.

The agreement leaves Australia facing decades of spending and industrial expansion, alongside the immediate challenge of maintaining its ageing submarine fleet until replacements arrive.

UN Security Council endorses Gaza ceasefire plan

UNITED NATIONS, June 10, 2024 — The United Nations Security Council on Monday endorsed a three-phase proposal to end the war in Gaza, urging Israel and Hamas to implement the plan without delay or conditions.

The U.S.-drafted resolution passed with 14 votes in favour and Russia abstaining. It welcomed the proposal announced by President Joe Biden on May 31, which Washington described as an Israeli offer, and called on Hamas to accept it.

The first phase envisages an immediate, full and complete ceasefire, the release of some hostages in exchange for Palestinian prisoners, and Israeli forces withdrawing from populated areas of Gaza. It also provides for civilians to return to their homes and neighbourhoods and for humanitarian assistance to reach them at scale.

A second phase would bring a permanent end to hostilities, the release of remaining hostages and a full Israeli withdrawal, subject to agreement by the parties. A third would involve a major reconstruction plan for Gaza and the return of the remains of hostages who died.

The resolution says that if negotiations take longer than six weeks during the first phase, the ceasefire would continue as long as talks continue.

Washington has linked an end to the war to broader diplomatic goals: supporting humanitarian efforts, protecting Palestinians and reviving talks on normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia. The council vote does not itself resolve differences between Israel and Hamas over how a ceasefire would become permanent.

The war began with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, which killed about 1,200 people, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent military campaign has devastated Gaza and displaced much of its population.

Japan adopts defence overhaul, plans long-range strike capability

TOKYO, Dec. 16, 2022 — Japan adopted a sweeping revision of its national security strategy on Friday, committing to a major military spending increase and the ability to strike targets abroad as it confronts growing concern over China, North Korea and Russia.

The plans envisage about 43 trillion yen in defence spending over five years and the acquisition of counterstrike capabilities, including U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles. Japan also plans to extend the range of its domestically developed Type 12 missiles.

The government aims to bring defence spending and related expenditure to 2% of gross domestic product by fiscal 2027, moving away from a longstanding benchmark of roughly 1%.

The strategy describes China's external posture and military activities as an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge to Japan's peace and security. North Korea's missile launches and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have also sharpened Tokyo's concerns.

Washington welcomed the overhaul, which strengthens the role of its principal treaty ally in East Asia. Beijing objected to the strategy's treatment of China. Military upgrades reflect regional anxieties, yet broader risks include deepening geopolitical estrangement.

Tokyo says the changes remain consistent with its exclusively defence-oriented policy under Japan's pacifist constitution. The government distinguishes counterstrikes in response to an attack from pre-emptive strikes, which it says remain impermissible.

Funding the expansion poses a domestic political challenge. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida has proposed covering the additional cost through a combination of spending reforms, other revenue and tax increases, drawing resistance even within his ruling party.

Australia, ASEAN urge restraint in South China Sea

MELBOURNE, March 6, 2024 — Australia and Southeast Asian leaders called for restraint in the South China Sea on Wednesday, concluding a summit amid renewed confrontation between Chinese and Philippine vessels in the disputed waterway.

A joint declaration issued after the three-day meeting urged countries to avoid unilateral actions that could endanger peace and stability. It called for disputes to be resolved peacefully in accordance with international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The summit marked 50 years of Australia's dialogue partnership with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a region central to Canberra's trade and security interests.

The declaration followed a confrontation near Second Thomas Shoal on Tuesday.
